title: Beisegel et al. Conjecture 1
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, every graph either is $P_k$-free or contains an avoidable $P_k$.
context_text: Beisegel et al. conjectured this generalisation of the known results for avoidable vertices (Ohtsuki et al. 1976) and avoidable edges (Beisegel et al. 2019, Theorem 1.4). It was also motivated by a result of Chvátal et al. 2002 establishing the same conclusion for $C_{\geq k+3}$-free graphs.
attributed_to: Beisegel, Chudnovsky, Gurvich, Milanič, and Servatius
paper_contribution: Proves the conjecture in full generality as Theorem 1.9, via a stronger induction hypothesis (Theorem 2.4), superseding all previous partial results.

title: Question 1.12
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, does every graph $G$ either not contain two disjoint $P_k$, or contain two disjoint avoidable $P_k$?
context_text: Cycles are induced unless stated otherwise, and $P_k$ means an induced path on $k$ vertices ($G$ is $P_k$-free if it has none). An extension of an induced path $P$ is an induced path $xPy$ for some vertices $x,y$; an induced path is failing if no induced cycle of $G$ contains it; and a path is avoidable if it is induced and has no failing extension. Thus an avoidable vertex is one such that every induced $P_3$ with middle vertex $v$ lies in an induced cycle (in chordal graphs, avoidable vertices are simplicial). The authors prove the conjecture of Beisegel et al. that for every $k$ every graph either is $P_k$-free or contains an avoidable $P_k$, and more generally that if $G[X]$ is connected then $G-N[X]$ is $P_k$-free or contains a $P_k$ that is avoidable in $G$. As a consequence, every graph either has no two non-adjacent $P_k$ or has two non-adjacent avoidable $P_k$. This question asks the analogue for (vertex-)disjoint copies. The answer is positive for $k\in\{1,2\}$ by results of Beisegel et al., but the paper itself answers it negatively for every $k\ge3$: take a cycle on $2k-1$ vertices plus a vertex adjacent to two consecutive cycle vertices; it has two disjoint $P_k$, which must be complementary and both meet the triangle, so one of them contains a single triangle vertex and has a failing extension. So the question is resolved, not open.
notes: The question is posed and then fully answered (negatively for $k \geq 3$) within the same paper; it is not open.

title: Question 4.1
statement_text: Does there exist a family $\mathcal{H}$ of connected graphs, not containing any path, such that any graph is either $\mathcal{H}$-free or contains an avoidable element of $\mathcal{H}$?
context_text: Cycles are induced unless stated otherwise, and $P_k$ means an induced path on $k$ vertices ($G$ is $P_k$-free if it has none). An extension of an induced path $P$ is an induced path $xPy$ for some vertices $x,y$; an induced path is failing if no induced cycle of $G$ contains it; and a path is avoidable if it is induced and has no failing extension. Thus an avoidable vertex is one such that every induced $P_3$ with middle vertex $v$ lies in an induced cycle (in chordal graphs, avoidable vertices are simplicial). The authors prove the conjecture of Beisegel et al. that for every $k$ every graph either is $P_k$-free or contains an avoidable $P_k$, and more generally that if $G[X]$ is connected then $G-N[X]$ is $P_k$-free or contains a $P_k$ that is avoidable in $G$. A graph is $\mathcal{H}$-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{H}$. The authors ask whether avoidability extends beyond paths. They note that for some structures the very notion of extension becomes unclear (what should an extension of a clique be?), and that no other structure seems to survive the test of chordal graphs or simple ad hoc constructions, even when a family of graphs is allowed instead of a single pattern. The notion of avoidability in this question is deliberately left up to interpretation by the authors. They also ask, more vaguely, when a graph admits three or more disjoint (or pairwise non-adjacent) avoidable paths, noting that the picture is murky already for chordal graphs.
